version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/swap: submit the last readahead batch before unplugging

patches_submitted.patch_summary: The patch addresses an issue where the last readahead batch is not submitted before unplugging, which can lead to unexpected behavior in block I/O operations. The fix involves moving the submission of the final batch before finishing the plug, ensuring that all batches are properly handled.

review_comments.author: Joshua Hahn
review_comments.summary: Found the patch reasonable and suitable for review. Raised a question about the need for the Fixes: tag, which Andrew Morton later clarified.

On Thu,  1 Oct 2026 10:57:12 +0200 Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr> wrote:

> Since block swap I/O is batched in struct swap_iocb, swap_add_folio()
> only appends a folio to the pending batch when its slot directly follows
> the previous one, and submits the pending batch otherwise. Batches
> submitted inside the readahead loop go through the plug, where the block
> layer can still merge them, but the final batch is submitted after
> blk_finish_plug() and always becomes a separate request.
> 
> So submit the final batch before finishing the plug.

Hi Alex,

I read through the code and this looks very reasonable to me.

Reviewed-by: Joshua Hahn <joshua.hahnjy@gmail.com>

> Fixes: dda8fb68b590 ("mm/swap: also use struct swap_iocb for block I/O")

My only question is whether we need the fixes tag, it seems like
dda8fb68b590 is still in mm-stable and not merged to linus yet.

Andrew, what do we usually do in these cases? I am wondering if it will
just become folded into the original commit or if this should still be
standalone.

Thank you both! Have a great day : -)
Joshua

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 1/7] mm: support promotion-only NUMA hinting scans
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new mode for NUMA hinting scans that only promotes pages to higher tiers without scanning the entire VMA. The global balancing mode is used to determine the intent of an individual protection walk, and the patch adds a new flag MM_CP_PROT_NUMA_PROMO_ONLY to select this promotion-only mode. The change-protection flags are built in task_numa_work() based on the balancing mode, and folio_can_map_prot_numa() derives the single-threaded private state at the point of use instead of adding another precomputed boolean to the protection-walk interface. This patch is required for memory-tiering fixes and must be accompanied by them when backported.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 2/7] mm: allow shared folios to be promoted to a fast tier
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series allows shared folios to be promoted to a fast tier, addressing issues with NUMA balancing and memory tiering. It introduces a new function `folio_numab_promotable` to determine whether a folio can be migrated based on its access time and source-tier test. The patch also renames the existing `folio_use_access_time` function to better reflect its purpose.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 3/7] sched/numa: scan read-only file mappings in tiering mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses an issue in the NUMA balancing code, where read-only file mappings are not scanned for promotion when tiering is enabled. The patch introduces a new walk type for each VMA based on the balancing mode snapshot taken in task_numa_work(). This change ensures that hot file folios on slow memory are retained and prevents east-west placement bouncing.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 4/7] sched/numa: separate VMA placement from scan continuation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the logic of VMA placement and scan continuation in the Linux kernel's scheduler. The existing helper function `vma_is_accessed` is renamed to `vma_needs_placement_scan`, which only checks if a VMA needs placement sampling, regardless of whether it's already mid-scan. This separation allows for more accurate tracking of VMA scans and enables PID-inactive VMAs to be scanned for promotion without being treated as evidence of placement eligibility.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 5/7] sched/numa: scan PID-inactive VMAs for promotion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series enhances the vma scanning logic in the Linux kernel's scheduler to promote hot memory tiers more effectively. The current implementation skips VMAs without recent PID activity, but this can lead to inefficient memory usage and performance issues. The patches introduce a new mechanism to bypass the PID scan filter for combined mode and restrict top-tier sampling to VMAs that need it.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses poor NUMA balancing behavior in a production deployment by modifying the VMA scan filters to no longer gate memory-tier promotion. The issue arises from the global balancing mode's inability to describe the intent of individual VMA/PTE walks, leading to suboptimal performance and high request latency. To resolve this, the patch series introduces promotion-only NUMA protection walks and derives private VMA state in the folio eligibility check. It also separates VMA placement eligibility from partial-scan continuation and scans PID-inactive VMAs for promotion. The patches are designed to be backportable and include cleanups of the touched NUMA-balancing code.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/4] selftests/mm: check sub-PMD ranges window by window in check_huge()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the check_huge() function in selftests/mm to count folios of a specific order within a range by checking each window individually, rather than counting all folios and comparing the total count to the number of huge pages. This change is necessary for preparing the use of check_huge() in khugepaged.c for collapse_order cases. The patch moves the existing logic from one window into a new function called is_range_backed_by_order(), which checks if a range is backed by folios of a specific order, and uses this function to count the folios within each window.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/4] selftests/mm: check collapse results through check_huge() only
series_items.patch_summary: This patch simplifies the way khugepaged checks collapse results by using a single callback function, check_huge(), instead of two separate methods. The change affects several self-test files and removes unused code. The goal is to make the code more consistent and easier to maintain.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/4] selftests/mm: check split results by position, drop gather_folio_orders()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the split_huge_page_test to check the results of a split by position, rather than just counting folios of each order in the range. It achieves this by checking that each PMD-sized part of the range came out as expected after a non-uniform split. The test also removes its own use of gather_folio_orders() and instead uses cached descriptors directly. This change requires every page to be present, which is acceptable since the test has already read the whole range.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes an unnecessary mmgrab() reference in the madvise_collapse() function, which is already holding a valid mm_users reference. The redundant mmgrab() call is dropped to simplify the code and avoid potential issues.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 02/13] mm/khugepaged: count collapses where khugepaged makes them
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged functionality to count collapses where it makes them, rather than relying on the caller to increment a shared counter. The daemon can now keep its own counter without needing to test who called the collapse function. This change simplifies the code and improves maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 03/13] mm/khugepaged: rename mthp_present_ptes bitmap to eligible_ptes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the bitmap 'mthp_present_ptes' in the mm/khugepaged module to 'eligible_ptes'. The name change reflects that a set bit in this bitmap indicates not only that a PTE is present, but also that it has passed various checks. This change does not introduce any functional changes and is intended to improve clarity of the code.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 04/13] mm/collapse: add collapse.h for the collapse interface
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new header file, mm/collapse.h, to separate the interface and implementation of the collapse feature from the khugepaged.c file. The collapse feature is used for page migration and memory compaction. The new header file defines an enum for scan results and a struct for control parameters, as well as two constants related to page table entries. This separation improves code organization and maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 05/13] mm/collapse: state what a collapse may do in the policy
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new struct called collapse_policy to store the policy decisions made by the caller before asking for a collapse. The policy includes limits on missing, swapped-out or shared PTEs in a window, as well as other settings such as whether to look at used ranges and how to handle MADV_FREE'd pages. The patch replaces scattered tests throughout the collapse path with reads from the collapse_policy struct, simplifying the code and removing the need for khugepaged to look up who called it. The policy is filled once per scan pass by khugepaged and once per call by MADV_COLLAPSE.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 06/13] mm/collapse: drop the collapse_possible() wrapper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes a wrapper function called collapse_possible() that simply forwards to another function called collapse_possible_orders(). series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 07/13] mm/collapse: name the per-table scan reset for what it resets
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the function collapse_control_init_scan() to collapse_scan_reset(), which more accurately reflects its purpose of resetting accumulated data for a scan, including node load, allocation nodemask, and eligible-PTE bitmap. This change is part of a larger effort to improve the naming conventions in the mm/collapse code and prepare it for further refactoring. The patch does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 09/13] mm/collapse: separate scanning a PTE table from collapsing it
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the scanning of a PTE table from collapsing it into two distinct functions: collapse_scan_pmd() and collapse_run_pmd(). The scan function determines whether a range is worth collapsing, while the run function performs the actual collapse. This change improves performance by reducing the number of times the mmap_lock is dropped and taken, and also simplifies the code by breaking down complex operations into smaller, more manageable pieces.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 10/13] mm/collapse: open-code collapse_single_pmd() in its two callers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the collapse_single_pmd() function by open-coding its behavior in its two callers, khugepaged and madvise_collapse(). The original function handled different lock behaviors for these callers, but since they already act on dropping the lock, it's more straightforward to handle this directly in each caller. This simplifies the code and prepares for future changes, such as moving madvise_collapse() out of khugepaged.c.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 11/13] mm/collapse: work out the orders a VMA allows once per VMA
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the way the kernel handles memory collapsing by allowing it to work out the allowed orders for a VMA only once per VMA, rather than once per PTE table. This is done by passing the mask of allowed orders from collapse_possible_orders() directly to the functions that need it, and sampling it once per VMA instead of once per table. The patch also ensures that changes to hugepage_vma_revalidate() are properly handled under the lock that produced the mask.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 12/13] mm/collapse: declare the collapse interface in collapse.h
series_items.patch_summary: This patch declares the collapse interface in collapse.h, which includes functions and variables related to collapsing huge pages. The interface is designed to be used by a caller that holds the mmap_lock for reading, and it involves three main steps: setting up control, scanning PTE tables, and running the collapse. The patch also renames hugepage_vma_revalidate() to collapse_vma_revalidate() and adds documentation comments to explain the purpose and behavior of each function. This is a preparation step for implementing MADV_COLLAPSE in madvise.c.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern about the collapse engine and callers being intertwined by proposing to separate them through policy and interface changes. The author plans to restructure in v2, but no specific fix is mentioned.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

[ This is the first of the cleanups I said I would front-load ]

There is no line between the collapse engine and the callers that ask for
a collapse.  khugepaged.c holds both, and they reach into each other.

 - Sixteen tests through the collapse path read cc->is_khugepaged to work
   out what they are allowed to do, when every one of those decisions was
   made by the caller before it asked.

 - collapse_single_pmd() does both halves of a collapse behind one call and
   drops mmap_lock somewhere in the middle.  Which of its paths dropped it
   is not something a caller can see, so it hands back a bool and the
   caller keeps track.

 - MADV_COLLAPSE's implementation -- the walk over the user's range, the
   per-PMD loop, the errno translation -- sits in khugepaged.c, which is
   the daemon's file.

So: draw the line.  State what a caller allows in a policy, split the call
in two with the lock as the boundary, and move the syscall to madvise.c.
What the engine offers is then three calls, with the lock state written
down against each, and a policy the caller fills for itself:

    collapse_control_init(cc)         once, before the first table
    collapse_policy_*(&cc->policy)    what this caller allows
    collapse_scan_pmd(vma, addr, ...) per table, under mmap_lock
    collapse_run_pmd(mm, addr, ...)   when a scan found work, no mmap_lock

The engine stays in khugepaged.c for now; what changes is that it has an
interface, and that neither half has to ask about the other.  madvise.c
gains the operation it should have had all along.

Changes since v3
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260916093145.4022188-1-kirill@shutemov.name/

 - Patch 5: the PTE limits come as two sets, struct collapse_limits for a
   PMD-sized window and one for anything smaller, and the strict_sub_pmd
   flag goes.  The warning for a max_ptes_none between 0 and the maximum
   moves to where khugepaged fills its policy.  The fields only one side
   reads are prefixed anon_ or file_.  collapse_policy_forced() is
   collapse_policy_madvise() (David).

 - Patch 8 is new: collapse_file() is called from collapse_single_pmd()
   rather than from inside collapse_scan_file(), so the file scan stops at
   the decision before the scan/run split.  The writeback retry and the
   tracepoint change move into it, so patch 9 is only the split (David).

 - Patch 9: no collapse_control_release().  It had nothing to release in
   this series; it comes back with the engine, where init allocates.  The
   check that the last scan was run stays at the top of collapse_scan_pmd()
   (David).

 - Patch 10: the changelog says why the lock boundary belongs to the
   caller (David).

 - Patch 11: both callers pass their TVA type as the literal it is rather
   than reading it back from the policy (David).

 - Patch 12: kerneldoc on every function collapse.h declares (David).

 - Acked-by from David Hildenbrand on 1-4, 6 and 7; Reviewed-by from
   Baolin Wang on 10.  Reviewed-by dropped from 5 and 9, which changed.

Changes since v2
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260910120238.2529819-1-kirill@shutemov.name/

 - Patch 8: the file scan returns SCAN_PTE_MAPPED_HUGEPAGE as it is and
   the run is handed what the scan returned, so it goes straight to
   retracting the PTE table when it sees it.  The scan_retract_only flag
   and the result round trip go, and the two copies of the file put become
   one helper (Zi).  Patches 9-12 follow the new signature.

 - Patch 8: mthp_collapse() and collapse_huge_page() read the orders and
   the referenced and swapped-out counts from collapse_control instead of
   taking them as arguments (Baolin).

 - Patch 11: each interface function is documented where it is defined,
   with the lock state on entry and exit.  The overview in collapse.h
   stays (Zi).

 - Reviewed-by from Zi Yan on 8 and 9, and from Zi Yan and Baolin Wang
   on 5 and 10.

Changes since v1
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/cover.1788533997.git.kas@kernel.org/

 - Rebased onto mm-new with Vernon Yang's tracepoint fixes in it.  Patch 8
   no longer merges the two calls to each scan tracepoint, since the base
   already has one; its changelog now says what the status field reports.

 - Patch 3: nr_occupied_ptes is nr_eligible_ptes, and the mthp_collapse()
   comment counts eligible PTEs too (Zi, Baolin).

 - Patch 4: no comments on the two constants (Baolin).

 - Patch 5: one line per policy field (Baolin).

 - Patch 8: the file side is split like the anonymous one (Zi).
   collapse_scan_file() runs under mmap_lock in the scan and only reads;
   collapse_file() runs in the run.  See Behaviour below.

 - Reviewed-by from Zi Yan and Baolin Wang on 1-4, 6 and 7.

Patches
=======

The first three stand alone and can be taken separately:

  1  drop the mmgrab() MADV_COLLAPSE has held since 7d8faaf15545
  2  count collapses in khugepaged's own walk, where the daemon's
     bookkeeping belongs
  3  rename cc->mthp_present_ptes to eligible_ptes, which is what a set
     bit means

Then the interface, in order:

  4  add collapse.h, and move enum scan_result, struct collapse_control
     and the two constants into it
  5  struct collapse_policy, filled by the caller; the is_khugepaged
     tests become field reads, and the flag goes
  6  drop collapse_possible(), a wrapper that only turns a mask into a bool
  7  collapse_control_init_scan() is a per-table reset, so name it
     collapse_scan_reset()
  8  call collapse_file() from collapse_single_pmd(), so the file scan
     stops at the decision
  9  give the scan and the collapse a function each: collapse_scan_pmd()
     and collapse_run_pmd()
 10  open-code the entry point that joined them, so each caller owns the
     lock across the boundary and the bool goes
 11  work out the orders a VMA allows once per VMA, not once per table
 12  declare the three calls in collapse.h, with the lock rules
 13  MADV_COLLAPSE moves to madvise.c

Behaviour
=========

No functional change is intended.  Nothing here changes which tables get
collapsed, into what, or what MADV_COLLAPSE returns.  The tracepoints are
the one place a change can be seen from outside; the rest is where work
happens, not what it does.

 - Patches 8 and 9: mm_khugepaged_scan_file and mm_khugepaged_scan_pmd
   fire before the collapse rather than after it.  For an accepted table
   their status field reads SCAN_SUCCEED, where it used to carry what the
   collapse made of the table; that is now for mm_khugepaged_collapse_file
   and mm_collapse_huge_page to report.

Four things move that a reader should not have to find in the diff:

 - Patch 5: khugepaged fills its policy once per scan pass, so the
   max_ptes_* limits and the defrag setting behind the allocation mask are
   sampled once per pass rather than once per table.  A knob written
   mid-pass takes effect on the next pass instead of the next table.

 - Patch 8: the writeback retry re-runs collapse_file() alone, where it
   used to rescan the page cache first.

 - Patch 9: the file scan runs under mmap_lock, where before the lock was
   given up first.  A file table the scan refuses no longer costs
   khugepaged an unlock, a trip back through khugepaged_do_scan(), a
   relock and a VMA lookup; only a table it goes on to collapse does.

 - Patch 11: which orders a table is scanned for is sampled once per VMA
   rather than once per table.  It cannot widen what a collapse does; the
   order is tested again under the lock the collapse retakes.

For an anonymous table, and for a file table that gets collapsed, the lock
is given up and taken again at exactly the points it was before; the only
difference is that the caller is the one doing it.

selftests/mm khugepaged passes on x86-64 with a KASAN, lockdep and
DEBUG_VM config, in the five forms run_vmtests.sh runs it.  Every patch
builds, CONFIG_TRANSPARENT_HUGEPAGE=n included.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the tight coupling between the users of collapse and its machinery in khugepaged.c, agreeing to separate them by introducing a new header file mm/collapse.h that defines common types and constants used by both sides. This change is non-functional.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern about the complexity of collapse_single_pmd() by splitting it into two functions: collapse_scan_pmd() and collapse_run_pmd(). The new functions are designed to work together, with collapse_scan_pmd() scanning for potential collapses and collapse_run_pmd() performing the actual collapse. The author also moved the anonymous scan under mmap_lock with the file scan, reducing the number of times the lock is taken.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed David Hildenbrand's concern about the PTE limits being set differently for PMD and sub-PMD windows by introducing a new struct collapse_policy that allows callers to specify their own policy, including PTE limits. The khugepaged code will fill in this policy once per scan pass, while MADV_COLLAPSE will do so once per call. This change does not alter the behavior of khugepaged but rather simplifies the logic by removing the need for the collapse code to look up who called it.

review_comments.author: David (Arm)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer David (Arm) noted that the patch changes the behavior of khugepaged by sampling max_ptes_* limits and defrag setting once per pass instead of on every table, which is a change in behavior. He also acknowledged two other changes as not actually required for the original call to collapse_file() from collapse_single_pmd().

review_comments.author: Andrew Morton
review_comments.summary: Andrew Morton requested that the collapse engine be separated from its callers, specifically suggesting that khugepaged.c hold only one half of a collapse and that the other half be moved to madvise.c. He proposed drawing a clear line between the two by introducing an interface for the engine and splitting the call into three parts: initialization, policy setting, and scanning/running.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Zi Yan noted that the original patch did not properly separate the scanning and running of collapses, with collapse_single_pmd() doing both jobs in the middle of a function. He suggested splitting this into two functions: collapse_scan_pmd(), which scans one table, and collapse_run_pmd(), which does the actual collapse work.

On Mon Sep 28, 2026 at 6:06 AM EDT, Kiryl Shutsemau wrote:
> From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>
>
> Tests scattered through the collapse path decide what a collapse is
> allowed to do by asking whether khugepaged started it.  Between them they
> settle:
>
>  - which VMAs are eligible, and how hard to try for a folio;
>  - how many empty, swapped-out or shared PTEs a window may contain, and
>    whether a sub-PMD window is held to a stricter rule than a PMD;
>  - whether a range has to look used, and whether a MADV_FREE'd page is
>    left alone;
>  - whether the PMD is mapped as part of the request, and whether dirty
>    pages are worth writing back and retrying.
>
> None of those is a fact about khugepaged.  Each is something the caller
> decided before asking, and the collapse code should not have to look up
> who called to find out.
>
> Add struct collapse_policy for the caller to fill: khugepaged from its
> own settings, MADV_COLLAPSE from the fact that a user asked explicitly.
> Every test becomes a read of a field, and cc->is_khugepaged goes, having

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/7] cgroup: add cgroup_account_system_time()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new helper function, cgroup_account_system_time(), which charges kernel CPU time to a cgroup's cpu.stat. The function is designed to be used in conjunction with the next patch, where it will be utilized for kernel threads working on behalf of other cgroups.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/7] cgroup: add set_active_cgroup() to charge CPU time to a cgroup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function called set_active_cgroup() that allows a kernel thread to charge its CPU time to a specific cgroup instead of its own cgroup, usually root. The function sets the task's active_cgroup field and returns the old value. It first charges the time used so far to the old cgroup before setting the new active cgroup. This is necessary for tasks like memcg reclaim from a workqueue that do work for a cgroup but are not part of it. Only kernel threads in the root cgroup can call this function, and it warns and does nothing if called by other processes. The patch also adds code to charge system time to the active cgroup when set under set_active_cgroup().

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/7] psi: charge pressure to the task's active cgroup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the Pressure Stall Information (PSI) system to charge pressure to a task's active control group when it stalls, such as during memory reclaim. The active cgroup is determined by the set_active_cgroup function and updated accordingly. When the active cgroup changes, the task's pressure state is moved from the old groups to the new ones, similar to how real cgroup moves are handled. This change ensures that PSI accurately reflects the pressure on a task's current control group.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/7] sched/fair: add cfs_bandwidth_charge() for kernel work done for a cgroup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function, cfs_bandwidth_charge(), which charges kernel work done by a task to its controlling cgroup's CPU time budget. The function takes into account the cgroup's own quota and that of its ancestors with limits, ensuring that the work does not starve the group for long. If the pool cannot cover the work, it becomes debt, paid out of subsequent refills. This change is necessary to accurately reflect kernel work done by a task in the cgroup's CPU time usage statistics.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 5/7] cgroup: take set_active_cgroup() time out of the cgroup's cpu.max
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the set_active_cgroup() function to charge kernel time used by tasks to their current cgroup's cpu.max quota, in addition to updating the task's active cgroup. This ensures that CPU usage is accurately accounted for and reflected in the cgroup's statistics. The change involves storing the task's runtime at each set_active_cgroup() call and then charging the old cgroup with the used time when the active cgroup changes.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 6/7] memcg: charge high_work reclaim to the memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the behavior of high_work reclaim in the Linux kernel's memory cgroup (memcg) subsystem. When a memcg exceeds its memory.high limit, the reclaim process is currently run from a kworker thread in the root cgroup, which means it doesn't get charged to the memcg's cpu.stat or memory.pressure metrics and doesn't count against its cpu.max quota. This patch changes the reclaim process to run under set_active_cgroup(), which charges its CPU time and memory stalls to the memcg's cgroup and deducts from its cpu.max quota, providing a more accurate representation of the memcg's resource usage.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 7/7] selftests: cgroup: check that high_work reclaim is charged to the memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two selftests to the Linux kernel's cgroup testing framework. The first test, `test_memcg_high_work`, checks that high-work reclaim is charged to the memory control group (memcg) by filling its TCP receive buffers from a softirq while only one task sleeps, causing the memcg to exceed its memory limit and triggering high-work reclaim. The second test, `test_memcg_high_work_cpu_max`, runs a CPU hog in the memcg under a cpu.max limit, ensuring that the hog gets less CPU time when high-work is busy. Both tests require swap space to be enabled so that anon memory can be reclaimed.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces a mechanism to charge kernel work to the cgroup it is being done for, rather than charging it to the root cgroup. This addresses a problem where CPU time spent by kernel threads on behalf of a specific cgroup is not accounted for in that cgroup's statistics and quotas. The approach taken involves allowing kernel threads to specify which cgroup they are working for, and then updating the relevant statistics and quotas accordingly. This will improve resource isolation and accuracy of accounting for CPU usage in various scenarios, including memory reclaim from high-work queues.

review_comments.author: Tejun Heo
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Tejun Heo noted that the current approach of moving a kworker into the target cgroup before running it has scalability issues due to contention on cgroup_mutex and cgroup_threadgroup_rwsem, and suggested an alternative direction for remote charging where a kthread explicitly specifies which cgroup the work is intended for.

Reviewer noted that the proposed solution does not address net rx, another major source of displaced CPU usage, and suggested adopting an approach that can cover both memory reclaim and net rx use cases by counting per-cgroup received packets and prorating CPU consumption.

Reviewer Tejun Heo expressed concern about the unconditional forgiveness of debt capping, suggesting instead that the cgroup should be slowed down to throttle new work generation and avoid out-of-control situations, similar to IO control mechanisms.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hello, Shakeel.

On Thu, Sep 24, 2026 at 11:47:04AM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:

---

This doesn't translate to net rx, which is another major source of
displaced CPU usage. Switching membership on each packet isn't going to
work there. Attribution can't happen that way. We'd much rather count
per-cgroup received packets and prorate the CPU consumption. If at all
possible, I think it'd be better to adopt an approach which can cover
both use cases.

---

I don't like the debt capping. Having debt doesn't have to mean that
the cgroup doesn't get any bandwidth at all. The cgroup just needs to
be slowed down enough that the generation of new work is throttled and
the whole thing doesn't go out of control. IO control already does
this: when IO debt is accumulated, userspace is heavily throttled, but
not completely stalled, until the whole cgroup's consumption comes
under control. I don't see why the debts would need to be forgiven
unconditionally. The cgroup can keep paying them while running at a
minimal rate to avoid triggering stall failures, and if the situation
doesn't resolve quickly, that will most likely trigger pressure based
kills in any reasonable setup anyway.

Thanks.

--
tejun

review_comments.author: Shakeel Butt (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author acknowledged a concern about accurate accounting of CPU time spent on network receive operations, particularly for modern NICs with dedicated rx queues and old NICs with shared queues. They proposed extending the mechanism to softirqs and considering a special way to account for the latter case, possibly through BPF.

Author agreed to address a concern about CPU time capping and promised to restructure it in the next patch version.
review_comments.raw_body:
Very good point. I think we need to think for net rx for two scenarios. First,
the modern NICs with rx steering support and second, old NIC with shared queues.

On the modern NICs where the workloads get their own rx queues, I think the
proposed mechanism can help to do the accurate accounting (I have to extend this
to softirqs as it is limited to kthreads atm) very easily.

The challenge you mentioned is for the old NICs where we get to know the cgroup
assosiation of the rx packets very late (or deep) in the stack. Also CPU spent
on each packet is not necessarily uniform (due to out-of-order or drops or
checksum errors or window shrinking) but for simplicity we can assume uniform
CPU. Maybe the right place to charge for such scenario might be at application
receiving those packets into the memory. I feel like we might need a very
special way to account for this case (maybe through BPF or something). At
the moment to me it seems very hard to have a universal solution which helps
this case and the reclaim case I am targetted.

If you don't mind, I think having solution for modern NICs i.e. dedicated rx
queues, should suffice for now (unless you want the solution for old NICs as
well). Let me know what you think.

---

Sounds good, I will remove this capping in the next version.

Thanks for taking a look.

review_comments.author: Tejun Heo
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Tejun Heo noted that the current approach to charging kernel work to a cgroup does not account for CPU time spent in common code for a specific cgroup, and requested remote charging of CPU time similar to IO and memory allocation.

Reviewer Tejun Heo expressed concerns that Rx steering is not suitable for attributing CPU cycles to each cgroup, citing its cumbersome setup and mismatched granularity.

Reviewer suggested combining net rx charging and reclaim CPU charging into a single mechanism where cycles are force-charged to the cgroup after the fact, without involving PSI.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hello, Shakeel.

On Thu, Sep 24, 2026 at 02:11:00PM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:

---

Rx steering is useful for partitioning the whole machine, but it doesn't
seem like the right tool for attributing CPU cycles to each cgroup. It's
cumbersome to set up and the granularity doesn't match. We aren't going
to be steering net rx processing per cgroup.

---

This doesn't have to be exact or completely synchronous. I don't see why
net rx charging and reclaim CPU charging can't share the same mechanism,
where the cycles are force charged to the cgroup after the fact.

I don't think PSI needs to be involved either. Shared execution in
itself shouldn't create pressure. The forced charge changes the cgroup's
usage, and that usage then creates pressure in the cgroup. IO works the
same way.

Thanks.

--
tejun

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 1/7] locking: add opt-in tracking of sleeping lock holders
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces an opt-in tracking system for sleeping lock holders in the Linux kernel. It allows tasks to count and report the number of locks they hold that have opted into this tracking, enabling a cheap way to check if a task is holding a lock that other tasks may be waiting for. This feature can help avoid stalls caused by memory allocation while holding shared locks, such as cgroup_mutex or kernfs_rwsem. The patch adds new APIs and infrastructure to support this feature, including a new header file and kernel configuration options.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 2/7] locking/rwsem: track holders of opted-in rw_semaphores
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a feature to track the holders of read-write semaphores (rw_semaphores) in Linux. It introduces a new flag, `tracked`, which is set when an rw_semaphore is opted-in for holder tracking. The count of holders is incremented when a task acquires the lock and decremented when it releases the lock. This feature is designed to help with debugging and troubleshooting by providing information about who holds a particular lock. It also includes support for PREEMPT_RT builds, which have a different locking mechanism. The patch modifies several kernel files to implement this new feature.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 3/7] locking/mutex: track holders of opted-in mutexes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a feature to track the holders of opted-in mutexes in Linux. It adds a function called `mutex_track_holder` that allows developers to opt-in mutexes for holder tracking. The function is used to count the number of locks held by a task, which can help identify potential bottlenecks and stalls in the system. The patch also includes changes to handle PREEMPT_RT builds and ensures that the tracking flag survives even after the lock has been released. The feature is opt-in, meaning it only applies to mutexes that have explicitly opted-in for holder tracking.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 4/7] locking/percpu-rwsem: track holders of opted-in percpu_rw_semaphores
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a feature to track the holders of percpu_rw_semaphores, which are used in various Linux kernel components such as filesystem freeze and async writes. The patch introduces a new function `percpu_rwsem_track_holder()` that allows opting-in percpu_rw_semaphores for holder tracking. It also updates several functions to count the lock holders correctly, ensuring that tasks are not preemptible while holding the lock without being counted. This feature is enabled by CONFIG_TRACK_LOCK_HOLDERS and adds a new field `tracked` to the percpu_rw_semaphore structure.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 5/7] locking/selftests: add KUnit tests for lock holder tracking
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds 16 KUnit tests to verify the lock holder tracking functionality in Linux. The tests cover various scenarios, including locks that did not opt-in, mutex and rw_semaphore calls, downgrade_write(), cleanup.h guards, nested locks released out of order, and percpu_rwsem_release()/percpu_rwsem_acquire() hand-off. Five tests use a helper thread to hold a lock and check the count, while three cases cover what the opt-in changes besides the count. The tests are designed to ensure that task_nr_tracked_locks(current) always equals the number of opted-in locks held by the task.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 6/7] Documentation/locking: document sleeping lock holder tracking
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds documentation to the Linux kernel's locking subsystem, specifically about sleeping lock holder tracking. The feature allows kernel code to identify tasks that are holding widely shared locks and may be causing stalls in other tasks waiting for those locks. It provides information on how a task can opt-in to being tracked, how the count is updated, and what it costs in terms of performance. The documentation also explains where each lock type updates the count and notes what is not covered by this feature.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RESEND 7/7] kernfs, cgroup: track holders of the cgroupfs locks
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the cgroupfs kernfs rwsems, cgroup_mutex and cgroup_threadgroup_rwsem by enabling lock holder tracking. This is done to prevent a stalled lock holder from stalling unrelated work in the cgroupfs control plane. The patch adds a new flag KERNFS_ROOT_TRACK_LOCK_HOLDERS that enables this feature for roots whose locks are shared widely across different operations, such as create, destroy and migrate. The patch also includes opt-ins for statically defined locks cgroup_mutex and cgroup_threadgroup_rwsem. This is part of a policy to read the count of lock holders, which should be implemented separately.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces a mechanism to track sleeping lock holders in the Linux kernel. It allows locks to opt-in to being tracked, and stores a count of these locks in task_struct. This is intended to help solve isolation failures caused by shared locks, where one workload's pressure can leak into another unrelated workload. The solution aims to improve performance by allowing the allocator to treat tasks holding widely shared locks differently, especially under memory or CPU pressure.

>
> This is the first series of memcg_ext, proposed at [1].  It adds
> bpf_memcg_ops, a struct_ops type through which memory controller policy is
> attached to a cgroup.  A charge runs the policies of its cgroup and of
> every ancestor, and the kernel combines what they return.  BPF picks
> between things the kernel already does; it never does the work itself and
> never touches a page counter.
>
> The plan is to grow this one member at a time, and to add a member only
> when there is a concrete problem it solves and a measurement showing it
> does.  Nothing is added because it might be useful later.  So this first
> series adds one member, for one problem.
>
> The problem
> ===========
>
> try_charge_memcg() calls __mem_cgroup_handle_over_high() before it returns,
> which reclaims and can throttle the task.  That happens wherever the charge
> happens, so a task holding a kernel lock can be stuck there, and everything
> waiting on that lock is stuck behind it.
>
> One concrete scenario which can be resolved by this new feature is the
> kernfs notify worker. It delivers notifications with the cgroup2
> kernfs_rwsem held for read, and the charge for the delivery allocation goes
> to the cgroup that set the watch, usually one already under pressure. So

should have a sane default behavior for memory.high. At the moment, if the
current charging process accumulates charges totaling more than

memory.high is enforced synchronously. You are suggesting that we should
increase the threshold from MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH to some arbitrarily large

rare.

I am fine with changing the default behavior. Actually, I have been
contemplating whether I should propose a revert of commit c9afe31ec443e

it has introduced more problems than it has solved, but that is a separate
topic. The initial commit already mentioned that MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH was used

greater maintenance burden as the kernel evolves, since the annotations

On Thu, Oct 01, 2026 at 08:42:55AM -1000, Tejun Heo wrote:
> Hello, Shakeel.
> 
[...]
> 
> > Here if you meant that default behavior of memory.high should work for most (if
> > not all) users then we are on same page. If some user want memory.high reclaim
> > to happen in a separate thread instead of return-to-userspace or synchronously,
> > this proposal provides mechanism through BPF to such users to achieve their
> > goals.
> 
> I think there's a common reasonable solution here, which is deciding by who
> the charge is for. A task charging for itself gets return-to-userspace
> enforcement plus the checks in the explicit bulk operations above. A kthread
> or anything else charging on behalf of a cgroup shouldn't be throttled for
> the cgroup's overrun. The overrun is attributed to the cgroup, async reclaim
> is kicked, and the cgroup's own tasks absorb the throttling on their next
> return to userspace. The in-charge synchronous fallback goes away. Each case
> has one reasonable answer, so I don't see a policy choice to expose here.
> 

Let me list the cases explicitly to see where we agree and where we disagree:

1. For the !in_task() charge path, today we trigger async reclaim and we will
   continue to do the same in the future.

2. For a kthread (or remote charging), today we throttle it similarly to user
   threads, but we want it to be handled similarly to the !in_task() case, i.e.
   trigger async reclaim. Regarding your statement "the cgroup's own tasks
   absorb the throttling on their next return to userspace", I assume you meant
   that when some other user thread of that memcg goes through the charge path,
   it will eventually do memory.high enforcement on return to userspace.

3. For a task, today we enforce memory.high on return to userspace, and if too
   much charge is accumulated in a single kernel entry, we enforce the high
   limit synchronously. You are suggesting that we remove the sync enforcement
   and add a couple of throttling points at known bulk allocation sites.

Please correct me if I misunderstood.

We are in agreement on (1) and (2) completely. For (3), I am fine with removing
the sync enforcement, but for throttling points for bulk operation sites,
I think we should only add them when there is an actual use case for that
or someone complains about overrun from those sites.

Now, setting aside the default behavior of memory.high, I want to provide
additional flexibility to users for (3) specifically. One specific case is
letting users opt in to async reclaim instead of the other forms of memory.high
enforcement. Basically, users can specify that instead of having their
application threads throttled, they would prefer async reclaim to bring their
usage back below memory.high. Whether we provide this functionality through
BPF or through something else, I am open to options.

thanks,
Shakeel

review_comments.summary: Tejun Heo questioned the necessity of introducing BPF policies for memory.high enforcement when most charges can be handled by raising the lazy bound or annotating specific paths that allocate large amounts of memory, and suggested that in-kernel synchronous enforcement is not necessary for kthreads charging on behalf of a cgroup.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hello, Shakeel.

On Mon, Sep 21, 2026 at 12:25:55PM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> try_charge_memcg() calls __mem_cgroup_handle_over_high() before it returns,
> which reclaims and can throttle the task.  That happens wherever the charge
> happens, so a task holding a kernel lock can be stuck there, and everything
> waiting on that lock is stuck behind it.

Why not just raise the lazy bound high enough that most charges never
enforce inline, and maybe annotate the specific paths that can allocate a
lot so that they do? Inline enforcement should be the exception, not the
rule. Flipping that and then trying to reverse it with custom BPF policies
doesn't make a lot of sense.

> One concrete scenario which can be resolved by this new feature is the
> kernfs notify worker. It delivers notifications with the cgroup2
> kernfs_rwsem held for read, and the charge for the delivery allocation goes
> to the cgroup that set the watch, usually one already under pressure. So
> the worker reclaims while holding the lock, a waiting writer blocks every
> later reader, and anything touching cgroupfs stalls for seconds.

Slowing down the kworker inline doesn't make sense. It's charging on behalf
of the watcher through set_active_memcg(), which already tells us whose debt
it is. Wouldn't it make more sense to defer the debt to that cgroup instead
of slowing down the kernel thread?

Thanks.

--
tejun

On Wed, Sep 30, 2026 at 06:28:21AM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> I am fine with changing the default behavior. Actually, I have been
> contemplating whether I should propose a revert of commit c9afe31ec443e
> ("memcg: synchronously enforce memory.high for large overcharges") because
> it has introduced more problems than it has solved, but that is a separate
> topic. The initial commit already mentioned that MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH was used
> arbitrarily, so replacing it with something big might be acceptable. I want
> to keep that decision separate.

Which kernel paths allocate enough for this to matter? Can you give specific
examples where the in-kernel synchronous enforcement helps?

> Returning to the actual proposal, my plan was to start small with a narrow,
> specific use case. However, my long-term plan is to provide a mechanism to
> change the default behavior for custom use cases. For example, for
> memory.high, I will provide a way for users to specify what behavior they
> want, i.e., whether or not they want more synchronous throttling.

This doesn't seem like a policy problem. It feels like a problem that should
be and can reasonably be solved for everybody, so I'm not sure whether BPF is
the right call for this specific purpose.

Thanks.

--
tejun

Hello, Shakeel.

On Wed, Sep 30, 2026 at 06:00:41PM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> mlock(), madvise(POPULATE), fadvise(WILLNEED) are the obvious ones where large
> amount of memory can be allocated before returning to userspace.

These are explicit bulk memory operations running in the calling task's own
context, so they can be special-cased. Each is a loop with points between
chunks where no locks are held, and the same over-high handler the
return-to-userspace path runs can run there. That keeps the throttling on
the task which asked for the memory and can't cause priority inversions. The
set of such paths is small and obvious, so I don't think it'd be onerous to
maintain.

> > This doesn't seem like a policy problem.
>
> What is "This" in the above statement?

The whole thing, how memory.high should be enforced when the overrun happens
inside the kernel or from a kthread.

> Here if you meant that default behavior of memory.high should work for most (if
> not all) users then we are on same page. If some user want memory.high reclaim
> to happen in a separate thread instead of return-to-userspace or synchronously,
> this proposal provides mechanism through BPF to such users to achieve their
> goals.

I think there's a common reasonable solution here, which is deciding by who
the charge is for. A task charging for itself gets return-to-userspace
enforcement plus the checks in the explicit bulk operations above. A kthread
or anything else charging on behalf of a cgroup shouldn't be throttled for
the cgroup's overrun. The overrun is attributed to the cgroup, async reclaim
is kicked, and the cgroup's own tasks absorb the throttling on their next
return to userspace. The in-charge synchronous fallback goes away. Each case
has one reasonable answer, so I don't see a policy choice to expose here.

Thanks.

--
tejun

series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a situation where an interrupt handler for the MPI3MR SCSI device returns without processing a reply queue, leaving it busy and unprocessed until the next interrupt or command timeout. To fix this, the patch sets a flag to enable polling of the reply queue when it is found busy, allowing the IRQ thread to process any pending replies.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] scsi: mpi3mr: Stop IRQ polling when no reply is ready
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the MPI3MR SCSI driver to stop IRQ polling when no reply is ready on a queue, reducing CPU usage and improving performance. The driver previously polled queues for about 45 seconds, waking every ~20us, which was inefficient. The change introduces an empty check while owning the queue, allowing the driver to switch back to interrupts once a poll finds the queue empty. This approach reduces the number of wakeups from 236 times per I/O to twice per I/O, resulting in significant CPU savings and improved throughput for certain workloads.
